source_title: Sample Interview: Telehealth, Trust and Regulation
text:
Host: Leila Haddad founded MedixCare in Cairo. Leila, tell us how it began.

Leila Haddad: I am a physician by training. I qualified in 2009 and practised for seven years, mostly in a public hospital in Cairo where I would see between sixty and eighty patients in a shift. A very large fraction of those visits did not require a physical examination at all. Someone had travelled two hours and waited five to be told to continue their medication. That is an enormous waste of the patient's life and of clinical capacity.

Host: So MedixCare started as video consultations?

Leila Haddad: We launched in 2018 as a scheduling and teleconsultation platform. And I will be honest, the first eighteen months were a failure. We had physicians on the platform and almost no patients. I assumed the problem was awareness and we spent money on marketing that did nothing.

Host: What was the actual problem?

Leila Haddad: Trust, and payment. Patients did not believe a consultation without a physical examination was real medicine, and there was no mechanism for insurance to cover it. We only started growing when we did two unglamorous things. First, we integrated with three private insurers in 2020 so the consultation was reimbursed rather than paid out of pocket. Second, we added a pharmacy fulfilment step, so the consultation ended with medication arriving at the patient's door. The consultation on its own felt like advice. The consultation plus the medicine felt like treatment.

Host: The pandemic must have accelerated things.

Leila Haddad: It did, enormously, and I am wary of taking credit for it. Monthly consultations went from about four thousand in February 2020 to sixty-five thousand by August 2020. But a lot of companies got that same wave and did not keep it. What mattered was whether you had built the reimbursement and fulfilment plumbing before the wave arrived, because you could not build it during.

Host: Where are you now?

Leila Haddad: We are operating in Egypt, Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. We have around three thousand two hundred physicians on the platform and we handled just over two million consultations in 2024. We raised a thirty-five million dollar Series B in 2022.

Host: What is the hardest part of the business?

Leila Haddad: Clinical quality control at scale. It is very easy to grow consultation volume and very hard to know whether the medicine being practised is good. We audit a random sample of consultations every week, we have a clinical review board, and we have removed physicians from the platform. That is uncomfortable and it slows growth and there is no version of this business where it is optional. If a telehealth company cannot tell you how it audits clinical quality, I would not use it.

Host: Advice for founders in regulated sectors?

Leila Haddad: Bring the regulator in early and bring them real data. We spent 2019 in conversations with the Egyptian health authority that produced nothing commercially and everything strategically. When teleconsultation guidelines were issued, they were written with an understanding of how this actually works, partly because we had been in the room. Founders treat regulation as something that happens to them. It is something you participate in.
